target: AG1's claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers for voters
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to give paid time off or close, so many low-income workers in retail, service, and similar jobs would still have to choose between missing pay and missing the vote.

target: AG1's claim that making Election Day a civic celebration would increase turnout
objection: The argument that a holiday would elevate civic participation is undermined by research indicating that an election-day holiday by itself is not a strong turnout strategy compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: AG1's implication that a national holiday is the best or sufficient solution to voting barriers
objection: More reliable approaches are targeted reforms such as requiring employers to provide paid time to vote, expanding early voting and vote-by-mail, and implementing automatic voter registration, because these directly address the actual barriers instead of assuming a holiday will change behavior.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday will not meaningfully reduce barriers because many employers will still be open and low-income workers may still face schedule conflicts
objection: A holiday does not have to solve every job situation to be useful; it meaningfully reduces the routine conflict between work/school schedules and Election Day, and it does so in a way that lowers the need for one-off workarounds.

target: AG2's framing of the issue as a choice between a holiday and other reforms
objection: This is not an either/or choice: early voting and paid leave can coexist with a holiday, which would still address the core problem that many voters face scheduling pressure on Election Day itself.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday only helps people whose employers already give paid time off
objection: That claim underestimates how holidays work in practice, because public services and many private workplaces scale back or close on major holidays, and international experience shows the approach is administratively workable.

target: AG1's reply that a holiday reduces schedule conflicts and is a useful baseline change
objection: Even if some offices scale back, the jobs held by many low-income workers—especially retail and service roles—often remain open on holidays, so the workers with the greatest burdens may still have to choose between voting and pay.

target: AG1's suggestion that school closures are a minor downside compared with the benefits of a holiday
objection: A holiday can create a new childcare barrier, because if schools and youth programs close while some parents still must work, they may face extra childcare costs or less supervision available to get to the polls.

target: AG1's reliance on OECD countries that hold elections on weekends or holidays as evidence the policy is workable
objection: International precedent is not decisive because those countries often have different labor and paid-leave regimes; without guaranteed paid time off, an election holiday is not the same policy package and will produce different real-world incentives.

target: AG2's claim that polling-operation improvements do not address voter access
objection: Improved staffing, logistics, and fewer disruptions at polling places do improve access because they can reduce long lines and the total time required to vote, which makes it less likely that workers must give up an entire shift.

target: AG2's claim that childcare concerns make a holiday a worse policy
objection: Childcare complications are not unique to election holidays, and the bigger existing problem is the direct tradeoff many voters face between voting and wages; a holiday changes the default calendar conditions and can reduce those wage-related dilemmas.

target: AG1's claim that smoother polling operations meaningfully improve access for workers
objection: Faster lines are not the same as being able to vote without losing pay, because the binding constraint for many low-income workers is that their jobs remain open and their shifts are not paid leave, not simply the minutes spent at the polling place.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday creates a uniform baseline across workplaces
objection: A uniform national holiday still does not force private employers to close or pay, so access can remain highly unequal and the real-world result can still be a patchwork of some workplaces accommodating workers and others not.

target: AG1's suggestion that a holiday would complement rather than crowd out stronger reforms
objection: Election Day holiday proposals can reduce pressure for more direct workplace-centered reforms, because policymakers and employers may treat the holiday itself as sufficient and thus have less incentive to adopt paid voting leave.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday cannot materially change employer behavior because some workplaces stay open
objection: Even without forcing every workplace to close, a federal holiday changes staffing and scheduling norms, reducing the chance that workers are assigned shifts on the one day they need to vote and limiting managerial discretion over that scheduling.

target: AG2's claim that polling improvements are irrelevant because workers still face long absences from work
objection: Shorter, smoother voting processes lower the total uninterrupted time a voter must take away from work, and for many workers that reduced time burden is what makes voting feasible without losing pay or needing extended leave.

target: AG2's concern that a holiday might substitute for paid-voting protections
objection: That concern assumes a false substitution; a holiday can serve as the baseline structural change while still being paired with paid voting leave and other targeted reforms that cover the remaining gaps.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday changes scheduling norms enough to matter
objection: Scheduling norms are not enforceable access: without a legal requirement for private employers to provide paid time off or actually let workers leave, low-income workers can still be scheduled and still lose wages to vote.

target: AG1's claim that smoother polling makes the time burden small enough to solve access problems
objection: The main barrier for many constrained workers is not just time at the polling place but whether they can leave a required shift at all and afford the lost wages, so faster lines do not fix the core problem.

target: AG1's suggestion that a holiday can simply be combined with paid-voting protections
objection: If the meaningful reforms are already paid voting leave and other enforceable access measures, then the holiday is redundant and adds uncertainty and uneven effects without directly solving the barrier.
